picks.name: The Wellness Optimizer
picks.why_plausible: Adaptogens are squarely a wellness-optimization purchase, and her affinities (wellness, supplements, organic_grocery) plus price_sensitivity: low fit a $40 premium functional beverage. She wants ingredient transparency and outcome focus, which the brand's adaptogen and no-hangover claims can honestly support.
lean_into: ingredient transparency on the adaptogen blend
outcome-focused: calm/focus without the next-day cost
premium quality worth paying for
avoid: implying clinical trial proof the brief doesn't claim
picks.ad_angle: Swap the nightcap for a functional drink that supports how you feel tomorrow morning — adaptogens, no alcohol, no hangover debt.

picks.name: The Gen Z Aesthete
picks.why_plausible: functional_beverages is a named affinity and self_treat/impulse occasions match; she is exactly the sober-curious, aesthetic-driven Gen Z drinker who wants something photogenic in hand. functional ingredients, clean label

picks.name: The Gifter
picks.why_plausible: Premium presentation and price_sensitivity: low make a sparkling NA drink a natural host gift or holiday bar addition, especially for the growing number of guests who don't drink. plan.summary:
Budget leans to the two checkouts where the purchase itself implies the product 
Studiogrid's self-care bookings and Pantrygood's clean-ingredient pantry restocks 
with Movewell, Daily Form and Kitchenly as tests; Pop & Sip and Swiftcart are out as beverage competitors.

recommended.name: Studiogrid
recommended.tier_reason: The score only credited generic wellness tag overlap; the notes show the purchase moment itself is a paid self-care booking (yoga/spa/class), which is exactly where an adaptogen NA drink is consumed and gifted, and the $42 basket sits right at the $40 offer.
recommended.rationale:
Someone who just booked a yoga class or spa session is mid-wellness-routine and 'actively spending on self-care and fitness' 
an adaptogen sparkling drink is the obvious next indulgence, at a matching $42 basket size with 13.6M impressions of high-income West/Northeast traffic.

evidence.quote: actively spending on self-care and fitness

recommended.risk: Service bookings aren't product purchases, so shoppers may be in a scheduling mindset rather than a shop-more mindset at confirmation.

recommended.name: Pantrygood
recommended.tier_reason: The tag map read this as generic grocery adjacency, but the notes describe the exact claim-responsiveness this brand sells on, and a case of sparkling functional drinks is a literal pantry line item on the order these shoppers just placed.
recommended.rationale: Organic pantry restockers who are 'Responsive to clean-ingredient, sustainability, and wellness claims' are the natural buyer for an adaptogen sparkling drink, and a $40 add-on is half their $86 basket.

evidence.quote: Responsive to clean-ingredient, sustainability, and wellness claims

recommended.risk: Grocery subscribers may prefer to add beverages to their existing basket rather than open a new DTC relationship.

test.name: Movewell
test.rationale: Fitness-engaged activewear buyers with 'Strong crossover with wellness and beauty' are a plausible sober-curious audience at 22M impressions, but the link is to who they are, not to what they just bought.

evidence.quote: Strong crossover with wellness and beauty

test.risk: An apparel checkout gives no beverage cue; conversion may rely entirely on demographic overlap.

test.name: Daily Form
test.rationale:
Supplement buyers already pay for adaptogens and the $38 basket matches the $40 offer, but the notes warn the 'Audience skeptical of unsubstantiated health claims' 
the no-hangover/adaptogen pitch is exactly what gets scrutinised here.

evidence.quote: Audience skeptical of unsubstantiated health claims

test.risk: Creative leaning on vague functional benefits could underperform badly with this science-forward audience; test a claims-substantiated version.

test.name: Kitchenly
test.tier_reason: Scored as off-category, but the tag map missed the meal occasion: someone who just bought dinner ingredients is choosing what to drink with that meal, and the notes describe a food-interested household at nationwide scale.
test.rationale:
Meal-kit buyers are 'Convenience-motivated but food-interested' and are planning dinners 
an NA sparkling drink is a natural pairing pitch, with 36M impressions to learn on.
test.risk: Family households skew less sober-curious than the target, and subscription checkouts often convert poorly on unrelated one-time offers.

launch_summary.summary: Of the $10,000 budget, $8,500 goes to two checkouts where the purchase itself sets up the offer: Studiogrid's self-care bookings and Pantrygood's clean-ingredient pantry restocks. The remaining $1,500 tests three adjacent audiences \u2014 Movewell activewear buyers, Daily Form supplement buyers and Kitchenly meal-kit buyers \u2014 to learn whether demographic or mealtime overlap can convert without a beverage cue. Beverage competitors Pop & Sip and Swiftcart are excluded.
uncertainties: The $40 first order value is assumed, and the $12.00 target cost per new customer is built on it, so a lower real price would make the whole plan overpay.
Daily Form's audience is noted as skeptical of unsubstantiated health claims, and the adaptogen and no-hangover pitch is exactly what gets scrutinised there.
The audience (sober-curious adults, roughly 25-45) and the one-time purchase model are both inferred or assumed, which affects both targeting and the payback math.
questions: What is your actual average first order value and margin?
Do you sell mainly one-time bottles or a subscription, and what is a customer worth over time?
Can you substantiate the adaptogen and no-hangover claims for a science-forward audience?
